short_description: Romano-Byzantine basilica atop Montmartre where candles have burned in perpetual prayer since 1885.

beats.script_body: On the night of October 5, 1914, a German bomb fell just meters from Sacré-Cœur but failed to explode. Parisians took it as a miracle — the basilica's perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament had been unbroken since 1885, and the congregation vowed it would never stop. It continues to this day.

On the evening of October 5, 1914, a German aerial bomb landed mere meters from Sacré-Cœur without detonating. The faithful saw divine protection — the basilica's perpetual prayer vigil, unbroken since 1885, had seemingly shielded it. That vigil of adoration continues around the clock even now.

short_description: The temple of the Republic — where France honors its greatest citizens.

beats.script_body: Voltaire was interred here in 1791, the first great man honored by the new Republic. The debates over who deserved burial in this secular temple reflected the ideals of the French Revolution and earned it the role of France's most sacred civic shrine.

It was Voltaire who was first laid to rest here in 1791, honored by the young Republic as a champion of reason and liberty. The fierce debates over who merited a place in this secular temple mirrored the revolutionary ideals of the age and established it as France's most hallowed civic monument.

Voltaire was interred in the Panthéon in 1791, the first citizen honored by the Republic. Revolutionary debates over who deserved burial here reflected France's deepest civic values. The building earned its role as the nation's most sacred secular shrine through those fierce arguments over merit and legacy.

short_description: The apartment where Victor Hugo wrote much of Les Misérables, on the Place des Vosges.

beats.script_body: Victor Hugo lived in this apartment on the Place des Vosges from 1832 to 1848. Built in the early 17th century, the Place des Vosges is the oldest planned square in Paris. From this writing desk, Hugo drafted large sections of Les Misérables.

short_description: Victor Hugo's historic 17th-century residence on the Place des Vosges.

beats.script_body: Hugo was more than a novelist — he was a poet, dramatist, and political activist. His funeral in 1885 drew two million mourners through Paris, and his body lay in state beneath the Arc de Triomphe before burial in the Panthéon.

short_description: Paris's most beloved public garden, created in 1612 for Marie de Médicis.

beats.script_body: Created in 1612 for Marie de Médicis, the Jardin du Luxembourg is the most cherished park in Paris. It served as a royal garden, a revolutionary assembly ground during the Terror, and even a Luftwaffe headquarters during the Nazi occupation.

short_description: Historic public garden — entered from the northeast corner near the Panthéon.

beats.script_body: The Grand Bassin at the center of the Jardin du Luxembourg has been a beloved gathering spot for centuries. Children push miniature sailboats across its waters with long sticks — a Parisian tradition dating back to the 1920s that continues every weekend.

short_description: The Sun King's palace — outside Paris geofence.

beats.script_body: Versailles began as a modest hunting lodge for Louis XIII in 1623. His son Louis XIV transformed it into the largest palace in Europe, housing 10,000 courtiers. On October 6, 1789, a Parisian mob marched here and forced the royal family back to Paris — they never returned.

short_description: Brussels' central square — outside Paris geofence.

beats.script_body: The Grand-Place was nearly destroyed by French bombardment in 1695, when Marshal de Villeroy's artillery flattened a third of Brussels. The guilds rebuilt their ornate facades within four years, creating the baroque masterpiece visible today.

short_description: William the Conqueror's fortress — outside Paris geofence.

beats.script_body: The Tower of London has served as a royal palace, prison, and execution site since 1066. The Crown Jewels have been guarded here since 1303, after a thief nearly stole them from Westminster Abbey.

short_description: Legendary Canal Saint-Martin bakery — home of the pain des amis.

beats.script_body:
Du Pain et des Idées has been baking in this 19th-century shop since Christophe Vasseur left his advertising career in 2002. The rivalry with Poilâne across the river is legendary — Parisians call it the "Bread Wars." Pro tip: try the pain des amis. It's Vasseur's secret weapon.

As Christophe Vasseur once said: "Bread is not a product — it's a living thing."

Le Comptoir du Panthéon brought modern bistronomy to the Latin Quarter in 2005. Chef Yves Cambeborde's philosophy: «la cuisine est un art» — cooking is an art. The restaurant's pièce de résistance was always the dégustation menu.

short_description: The island birthplace of Paris — testing invalid lens values.

beats.script_body: The Île de la Cité was once home to a medieval labyrinth of streets so cramped and disease-ridden that Baron Haussmann demolished nearly everything in the 1860s. Today only Notre-Dame, the Conciergerie, and Sainte-Chapelle survive from that ancient city within a city.
The Conciergerie on the Île de la Cité served as the chief prison during the Reign of Terror. Marie Antoinette spent her final days in a tiny cell here before her execution in 1793.

short_description: The start of the 1.9-kilometer Champs-Élysées — testing 12-beat max.

beats.script_body: Hidden history beat for the Champs-Élysées. The tree-lined promenade was originally open fields and market gardens until Marie de Médicis extended the Tuileries vista in 1616.
Architecture beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue passes grand Haussmann-era buildings, each with distinct facades spanning Second Empire to Art Nouveau styles.
Local legends beat for the Champs-Élysées. Legend has it the ghost of a Napoleonic cavalry officer rides down the avenue at midnight on the anniversary of Austerlitz.
Food beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue's side streets hide classic bistros and pâtisseries dating back to the Belle Époque of the 1890s.
Art beat for the Champs-Élysées. Street artists sketch caricatures of passersby near the Grand Palais, continuing a tradition from the 19th-century Salons.
Dark history beat for the Champs-Élysées. During the Occupation, Nazi soldiers paraded down this avenue daily — and after Liberation in 1944, suspected collaborators were marched here in shame.
Literary beat for the Champs-Élysées. Proust, Hemingway, and Baudelaire all wrote about these boulevards and the café life that thrived along them.
Religious beat for the Champs-Élysées. Three of Paris's most important churches lie nearby: La Madeleine, Saint-Philippe-du-Roule, and the American Cathedral.
Music beat for the Champs-Élysées. 'Les Champs-Élysées' by Joe Dassin became an international hit in 1969 and is still the avenue's unofficial anthem.
Revolutionary beat for the Champs-Élysées. Every Bastille Day, the avenue hosts the largest military parade in Europe, commemorating the storming of the Bastille in 1789.
Nature beat for the Champs-Élysées. Green bookends: the Jardin des Tuileries on one end and the Bois de Boulogne beyond the Arc de Triomphe.
Shopping beat for the Champs-Élysées. The avenue has been a commercial hub since the mid-19th century, home to Louis Vuitton, Cartier, and Guérlain.

short_description: Paris's most ornate bridge — testing content length extremes.

beats.script_body: Short.

The Pont Alexandre III, spanning the Seine between the Grand Palais and Les Invalides, is widely considered the most ornate bridge in Paris. Designed by Joseph Cassien-Bernard and Gaston Cousin and built between 1896 and 1900 for the Universal Exposition, it was named after Tsar Alexander III to celebrate the Franco-Russian Alliance of 1892. The bridge was an engineering marvel — a single steel arch spanning 107 meters, kept intentionally low so as not to obstruct the view of the Champs-Élysées or Les Invalides. During construction, workers discovered remnants of an older wooden footbridge from the 17th century buried in the riverbed. The bridge's four gilded bronze Fames statues on towering pylons represent the Sciences, the Arts, Commerce, and Industry. A time capsule sealed by Tsar Nicholas II during the foundation ceremony in 1896 is believed to still be embedded in the right-bank abutment. The bridge offers some of the most spectacular views in Paris, framing the dome of Les Invalides on one side and the glass roof of the Grand Palais on the other, making it a perennial favorite of photographers and filmmakers. Guy de Maupassant, who despised the Eiffel Tower, reportedly said this bridge was the only structure in Paris worthy of the new century.

short_description: Masterpiece of Charles Garnier — testing review band (30-69% Jaccard).

beats.script_body: The Opéra Garnier was designed by Charles Garnier and completed in 1875. The Beaux-Arts style was so influential it defined an entire era of Parisian architecture. The building sits on an underground lake that inspired Gaston Leroux's Phantom of the Opera.

Charles Garnier's Opéra, finished in 1875, defined the Beaux-Arts style that would dominate French architecture for decades. The massive structure rests above a subterranean reservoir because the water table was too high to drain during construction. Marc Chagall's ceiling mural, painted in 1964, caused an uproar — critics called it a modernist insult to a classical masterpiece, but it is now considered one of Paris's great treasures.

short_description: One of the oldest public libraries in France, with roots in a 6th-century abbey.

beats.script_body: The Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève traces its origins to the Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève, founded in the 6th century. Henri Labrouste's 1851 iron-and-glass reading room stretches 84 meters — one of the most magnificent library interiors in the world.

The library's facade is inscribed with 810 names of great authors and scientists, carved into the stone by Labrouste himself. The collection holds manuscripts dating back to the Carolingian era — some over a thousand years old.

short_description: A former railway station transformed into the world's greatest Impressionist museum.

beats.script_body: The Musée d'Orsay was originally the Gare d'Orsay, a Beaux-Arts railway station built for the 1900 Universal Exhibition. By 1939 its platforms were too short for modern trains and it fell into disuse. President Giscard d'Estaing saved it from demolition in 1977 and converted it into a museum.

The museum sits on the Left Bank of the Seine, on the site of the old Palais d'Orsay, which was burned down during the Paris Commune of 1871. The giant station clocks on the facade have become iconic — from behind, they frame perfect views of Montmartre.

short_description: The cathedral of clay-court tennis, opened in 1928.

beats.script_body: Roland-Garros was built in 1928 specifically to host France's defense of the Davis Cup after the "Four Musketeers" won it in 1927. It is the only Grand Slam played on red clay — the terre battue made from crushed brick quarried in the suburbs of Paris.

short_description: Home of the French Senate beneath a gilded dome.

beats.script_body: The Palais du Luxembourg was built for Marie de Médicis between 1615 and 1631, modeled after the Palazzo Pitti in Florence. During the Revolution it became a prison — Danton and Desmoulins were held here before their execution. It has housed the French Senate since 1799.
